Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Apex Capital Management Q3 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question and answer session. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Apex Capital Management's Q3 results. Joining me on today's call are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; John Harlan, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Investment Officer; David Patel, Head of Distribution; and Emily Vargas, Head of Operations.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that some of the statements made today may be forward-looking. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of the risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us. I'm pleased to report on our performance for Q3. We achieved solid results this quarter, driven by resilient market conditions and strong client demand across our diversified platforms. Our AUM grew to $1.28 trillion.

John Harlan: Thank you, Michael. From a financial perspective, Apex Capital Management delivered strong results in Q3. Our revenue was $1.42 billion, representing a 18% increase year-over-year. This growth was primarily driven by robust net inflows, market appreciation, and a favorable mix shift toward higher-margin alternatives and performance fees. Our expenses were $950 million, resulting in net income of $320 million. Our expense ratio improved due to scale efficiencies and technology investments.

Good morning, everyone. As we wrap up a resilient quarter amid ongoing market volatility, I'd like to dive deep into our assets under management—or AUM—and flows performance, providing color on the drivers and our forward guidance for Q4 2023 and the full fiscal year 2024. I'll break this down by key components: ending AUM, flow dynamics, market impacts, product and regional breakdowns, and the strategic levers we're pulling to drive long-term organic growth.

First, let's recap Q3 results. We closed the quarter with $1.28 trillion in AUM, up 4.2% quarter-over-quarter and 12.5% year-over-year. This reflects a combination of strong market appreciation—our portfolios captured about 105% of the MSCI World Index return on an organic basis—coupled with robust net inflows of $18.2 billion. Year-to-date through Q3, cumulative net flows stand at $52.4 billion, putting us on track for our strongest full-year inflow generation since 2021, when we hit $68 billion amid the post-COVID rotation into risk assets.

Breaking down the flows by asset class, equities led the charge with $12.5 billion in net new money, driven primarily by our suite of active and smart-beta ETFs. Our flagship Apex Global Equity ETF (ticker: APEQ), which has outperformed the S&P 500 by 250 basis points YTD on a NAV basis, saw $8.2 billion in retail inflows alone, fueled by advisor reallocation from cash proxies amid the Fed's pivot signaling. Fixed income added $4.8 billion, with short-duration and IG credit strategies resonating as yields stabilized around the 4.5-5% range; our Apex Ultra-Short Bond Fund pulled in $3.1 billion from institutional defined contribution plans. Alternatives were modestly positive at $1.2 billion, anchored by evergreen private credit commitments from family offices, though we saw some tactical outflows from direct PE as vintage year 2020-2021 realizations accelerated. Multi-asset and cash equivalents rounded out flat at -$0.3 billion, reflecting seasonal rebalancing.

Market performance contributed $42.7 billion to AUM growth in Q3, or about 3.4% on average AUM, benefiting from the AI-driven tech rally—where our quant-enhanced strategies in the Nasdaq-100 space added alpha—and a softer dollar that boosted our international exposures by 120 basis points on an FX-neutral basis. Fees benefited accordingly, with our blended fee rate holding steady at 42 basis points, down just 5 bps YoY due to targeted ETF scaling, but offset by higher-margin alternatives mix shift now at 18% of total AUM, up from 14% a year ago.

Regionally, North America remains our growth engine, delivering $13.9 billion or 76% of Q3 flows, with wirehouse channels like Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch platforms contributing over half via model portfolio approvals for our ESG-tilted SMA sleeves. EMEA flows were solid at $2.8 billion (15%), led by UCITS-compliant equity funds amid ECB rate cut expectations; our London-based team secured a €1.2 billion mandate from a Dutch pension fund for sustainable infrastructure debt. APAC added $1.5 billion (8%), with Hong Kong and Singapore retail platforms driving ETF adoption—our Apex Asia ex-Japan Equity ETF hit $500 million AUM milestone—though China exposure remains cautious at under 5% of regional book amid property sector headwinds. Emerging markets ex-China were a bright spot with $0.4 billion from LatAm sovereign wealth flows into our local currency EM debt strategy.

Strategically, we're leaning into several technical initiatives to sustain this momentum. First, our ApexFlow digital platform, now live with 1.2 million advisor users, has accelerated retail flows by 25% YoY through AI-driven personalization—think recommendation engines suggesting tactical overlays based on client risk scores and VIX regimes. We've also ramped up our tokenized fund pilots on blockchain rails with partners like BlackRock's BUIDL ecosystem, launching a $200 million private credit token for qualified institutional buyers, which enhances liquidity and reduces settlement T+2 to near-real-time. On the product side, we're guiding toward $10-15 billion in new launches by year-end, including three active ETFs targeting the 'Magnificent Seven' rotation and narrowing small-cap discount (Russell 2000 trading at 12x forward P/E vs. historical 16x), plus expanding our GP Stakes platform into secondaries with $5 billion deployment capacity.

Now, turning to guidance. For Q4 2023, we expect AUM to reach $1.35-$1.40 trillion, implying quarter-end flows of $15-25 billion net positive. This assumes MSCI World returns of 2-4% (beta-adjusted for our 1.02 portfolio beta), with equities continuing to attract 60-70% of flows amid year-end tax-loss harvesting and 401(k) contributions peaking in December. Fixed income should contribute $4-6 billion as the yield curve bear-flattens post-Fed cuts—we've already seen $2 billion in pre-funding for our new TIPS ladder ETF. Alternatives may moderate to $1-2 billion as fundraising cycles elongate in a higher-for-longer rate environment, but our evergreen structures mitigate this.

For full-year 2024, our core guidance is net flows of $70-85 billion, driving AUM toward $1.55-$1.65 trillion by year-end, a 21-29% increase. Organic growth target remains 4-6% ex-markets, above our long-term peer average of 3.2%, supported by 10-15% institutional mandate pipeline conversion (e.g., $20 billion from US public pensions rotating into privates). Upside risks include accelerated fee compression relief if active equity outperformance persists—our ex-post info ratio now at 0.45 across core strategies—and deeper APAC penetration via tie-ups with Temasek-linked platforms. Downside would stem from prolonged geopolitical flares, like Middle East tensions spilling into energy markets, or a US recession delaying DC plan flows.

We're well-positioned with a diversified flow base—60% recurring institutional, 40% higher-velocity retail/ETF—and balance sheet flexibility for strategic M&A, like bolt-on ETF issuers in the $10 trillion global ETF market growing at 15% CAGR. As always, forward-looking statements are subject to risks including market volatility, regulatory changes like SEC ETF transparency rules, and competitive dynamics from giants like Vanguard and BlackRock.

Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Moving now to our performance fees realized and a deep dive into our investment performance versus key benchmarks. As you know, performance fees—or incentive fees, as we sometimes call them—remain a cornerstone of our revenue model, particularly in our alternative strategies and long-only funds with hurdle rates. They align our interests with clients, rewarding true alpha generation above high-water marks and benchmarks.

In Q3 2023, we realized $178 million in performance fees, a robust 32% increase year-over-year and up 15% sequentially from Q2. This brings our year-to-date performance fee haul to $612 million, surpassing our internal target and representing about 18% of our total fee revenue. The surge was driven primarily by crystallization events in our hedge fund composites and private markets vehicles, where AUM under performance fee arrangements grew 14% to $92 billion over the year. Key contributors included our Apex Long/Short Equity Fund, which hit its high-water mark post a 22% NAV return, triggering a 20% carry on gains above the 8% hurdle; and our Global Credit Opportunities Fund, which locked in fees on $4.2 billion of deployed capital amid favorable dislocations in high-yield markets.

Looking at trends, we've seen a meaningful shift: performance fees from alternatives now comprise 62% of the total, up from 55% prior year, reflecting both organic alpha and $18 billion in net inflows into our fee-generating strategies. Fee compression in beta strategies continues, but our watermark-protected structures have held firm at an average 18% rate, well above peers like BlackRock's alternatives at 16% or KKR's 17%. Regionally, EMEA drove 28% of Q3 realizations, fueled by our London-based European Long/Short platform outperforming the STOXX Europe 600 by 450bps, while APAC contributed 22% via EM debt alpha in our Asia Ex-Japan Credit Fund.

Pivoting to performance versus benchmarks—a critical measure of our value-add. Across our $285 billion AUM as of quarter-end, our flagship strategies delivered compelling risk-adjusted returns, with an average Sharpe ratio of 1.42 over the trailing 12 months, beating the industry median of 1.18 per Morningstar data.

Equities first: Our Core Equity Composite returned 28.4% for the year-to-date, outpacing the S&P 500's 26.3% by 210bps. This edge came from tactical overweighting in AI and semiconductors—think Nvidia and TSMC positions scaled via our proprietary quant momentum screens—while underweighting cyclicals amid China slowdown risks. The Pinnacle U.S. Large Cap Growth Fund led with 32.1% net returns, +420bps over its Russell 1000 Growth benchmark, thanks to low-vol factor tilts that capped max drawdown at 11% versus the index's 15%. In EMEA, our Pan-European Equity Fund returned 19.2% gross, +310bps over MSCI Europe, benefiting from defense and renewables rotations. APAC was mixed: our Japan Equity strategy crushed the TOPIX at 24.7% versus 18.9%, driven by Abenomics 2.0 plays, but EM equities lagged MSCI EM by 50bps at 12.3%, hit by property sector de-risking in China.

Fixed income: A tougher environment with the Fed's hawkish pivot, but we navigated well. Our Aggregate Bond Composite yielded 4.8% for the year, trailing the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Aggregate Bond Index's 5.5% by just 70bps—far better than the category average underperformance of 120bps. Active duration management was key: we shortened to 5.2 years versus the Agg's 6.1, dodging the long-end selloff, while opportunistically adding 15% to securitized products like CMBS, which returned 7.2%. The Apex Total Return Bond Fund shone at 6.1%, +60bps over benchmark, via our AI-enhanced credit selection model that flagged undervalued BBB corporates from names like Ford and AT&T. In Europe, our Euro Aggregate strategy matched the Bloomberg Euro Agg at 3.9% but with superior yield-to-worst at 2.8% versus 2.4%, underscoring our focus on income over total return in a yield-starved region.

Alternatives and multi-asset: Here, we generated outsized alpha. Our Hedge Fund Composite returned 14.2% net, +720bps over the HFRI Fund Weighted Composite Index's 7.0%, with market-neutral quant strategies contributing 40% of gains via machine learning overlays on volatility surfaces. Private equity realizations hit 2.1x MOIC on exits from portfolio companies in fintech (e.g., our stake in Adyen-like platforms) and renewables. Multi-asset solutions, like our Pinnacle Balanced Allocation Fund, delivered 15.6% versus a 60/40 benchmark's 14.2%, blending 65/35 equity/fixed with 10% alts for enhanced convexity.

Strategically, these results stem from three initiatives: First, our next-gen alpha lab, deploying NLP and satellite data for real-time sentiment in EM equities, which added 80bps to APAC performance. Second, ESG integration without style drift—our sustainable equity sleeve outperformed MSCI World ESG Leaders by 150bps via carbon-efficient tech picks. Third, we're expanding hurdle structures with "catch-up" clauses to accelerate fee crystallization, targeting $750 million in 2024 performance fees amid expected rate cuts and equity dispersion.

Regionally, U.S. strategies remain our bedrock at 55% of AUM, but we're scaling EMEA to 25% with Dublin-domiciled UCITS launches, capitalizing on MiFID II flows. APAC growth hinges on Singapore hubs for wealth platforms, where we've won $5 billion in mandates post outperformance.

Before we open the line for questions, I'd like to provide our forward-looking guidance for Q4 2023 and the full fiscal year 2024. Our guidance reflects a constructive macro environment, with U.S. equities delivering mid-teens returns year-to-date amid resilient economic growth, while fixed income has benefited from the Fed's recent cuts and expectations of a 'higher-for-longer' rate path. We're also seeing robust demand for alternatives and ESG strategies, though fee compression persists in core beta ETFs, similar to trends at BlackRock and State Street.

Overall, we expect adjusted operating revenues of $1.45 billion to $1.50 billion for Q4 2023, up 8-11% quarter-over-quarter, driven by AUM expansion and modest performance fee realization. For full-year 2024, we guide to adjusted operating revenues of $6.20 billion to $6.50 billion, implying 10-14% growth over FY2023, with roughly two-thirds from organic AUM growth and the balance from institutional mandates and our recent $15 billion seed capital commitment to our private credit platform, Apex Direct Lending Fund II.

Management and advisory fees, which comprised 85% of Q3 revenues at $1.12 billion, are projected at $1.25 billion to $1.30 billion in Q4, reflecting average AUM of $1.85 trillion to $1.90 trillion. This assumes quarterly net inflows of $40 billion to $50 billion, led by $25 billion in U.S. long-duration fixed income ETFs (e.g., our ALFX flagship, up 22% AUM YTD) and $15 billion in APAC equities, where we've captured 150 bps of market share in active strategies amid China's stimulus rally. Fee rates should hold steady at 38-40 bps blended, though we'll see 5 bps compression in passive U.S. equity sleeves due to Vanguard-style price wars. For FY2024, we target AUM of $2.0 trillion to $2.1 trillion, with 6-8% organic growth from recurring retail flows via our robo-advisor platform, Apex Digital, now serving 4.5 million users with AI-driven model portfolios.

Performance fees at $120 million to $150 million in Q4 (up from $85 million in Q2), primarily from our $180 billion alternatives franchise, including private equity and infrastructure. We'll recognize ~200 bps on carried interest from three realizations in Apex Infrastructure Partners IV, which returned 18% net IRR vintage-to-date, outperforming Blackstone's BREIT amid stabilizing cap rates. FY2024 guidance is $550 million to $650 million, boosted by our new $10 billion evergreen private credit vehicle, seeded with pension flows from CalPERS analogs.

Other revenues, including administration and distribution fees, at $80 million to $90 million in Q4, supported by 15% growth in our BDC platform (Apex Business Development Company, yielding 9.5% dividend) and FX hedging spreads.

Shifting to expenses: We remain disciplined on cost management, guiding adjusted operating expenses to $1.05 billion to $1.10 billion in Q4, a 7-10% sequential increase but only 4% above prior-year Q4 on an apples-to-oranges basis. Our non-comp expense ratio improves to 22% of revenues, down from 24% in Q2, reflecting scale efficiencies.

Compensation and benefits at $650 million to $675 million in Q4, or 45% of revenues, flat sequentially as we lap prior-year variable comp accruals. Portfolio manager incentives tie 60% to alpha generation (e.g., beating Russell 3000 by 250 bps in our active growth fund) and 40% to net flows. For FY2024, we expect comp at 43-45% of revenues, with $150 million in deferred equity grants vesting over three years to retain our 1,200 investment professionals.

Distribution and servicing at $150 million to $160 million, up 5% due to higher third-party commissions on ETF sales via Schwab and Fidelity platforms. We're optimizing here with our proprietary ApexOne OMS, reducing sub-advisory leakage by 15%.

General and administrative (G&A) at $180 million to $190 million, including $40 million in tech capex for Phase 2 of our Aladdin-like risk analytics platform, Apex Sentinel. This integrates GenAI for real-time ESG scoring and predictive flow modeling, targeting 20% reduction in operational alpha drag—similar to Fidelity's recent AI hires.

Amortization and other at $70 million, steady, tied to our recent acquisition of a European quant shop.

Regionally, North America drives 65% of revenues with stable 40 bps fees, but we're accelerating EMEA growth to 20% of mix (from 17%) via UCITS-compliant alternatives, capitalizing on 11% AUM momentum post-MiFID II tweaks. APAC, now 15% of AUM, expects 25% revenue growth in 2024 from Japan GPIF rebalancing into illiquids.

Strategically, our 2024 playbook emphasizes three pillars: (1) Alternatives scale-up to 25% of AUM (from 20%), targeting $100 billion in GP stakes and co-invests with sovereign wealth funds; (2) Tech-led efficiency, with $250 million FY24 investment in blockchain custody for tokenized funds, positioning us ahead of SEC ETF approvals like BlackRock's Bitcoin vehicle; and (3) Organic flow machine, leveraging 95% client retention via personalized alternatives feeders.

This guidance embeds Q4 adjusted operating margin of 28-30% (up from 26% in Q2) and FY2024 margins of 32-34%, with EPS of $4.85 to $5.15. Risks include prolonged equity volatility capping performance fees or accelerated fee wars, but our diversified book—with 40% fixed income, 30% equities, 20% alts, 10% multi-asset—derisks us effectively.

Good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our core flow dynamics, which remain a key indicator of client confidence and our competitive positioning in the $120 trillion global asset management industry. For the quarter ended September 30, 2023, we recorded total net inflows of $18.4 billion, marking our 11th consecutive quarter of positive flows and representing a robust 28% increase year-over-year from $14.3 billion in Q3 2022. This brings our year-to-date net inflows to a record $62.7 billion, up 35% from the prior year, and underscores the resilience of our franchise amid a volatile macro environment characterized by persistent Fed tightening, geopolitical tensions in Europe, and the AI-driven equity rally.

Channel mix: Institutional flows led at $12.1 billion (66% of total), driven by $4.2 billion in long-term mandates from defined benefit pension plans and sovereign wealth funds, including a landmark $1.5 billion allocation from a Middle Eastern SWF to our multi-asset credit strategies. This reflects our strength in alternatives, where we captured 15% market share in private credit deals per Preqin data. Retail and intermediary channels contributed $6.3 billion (34%), with strong uptake via platforms like Schwab and Fidelity, bolstered by our fee compression on core ETFs—now averaging 12 basis points.

By asset class, flows were diversified but skewed toward high-conviction growth areas: ETFs $9.8 billion net inflows (53% of total), fueled by launches like our PEAK U.S. Tech Innovation ETF (PIXT), which gathered $2.1 billion since inception in July, capitalizing on the Nvidia-led AI surge. This compares favorably to BlackRock's iShares flows, where we're gaining 200 bps in tech equity ETF AUM share. Alternatives: $4.5 billion (25%), with $2.8 billion into private markets via our evergreen funds—private equity and infrastructure up 40% YoY amid yield-hungry LPs seeking 8-12% IRRs in a 5% risk-free rate world. Fixed Income: $3.2 billion (17%), rebounding from summer outflows as investors rotated into short-duration and EM debt amid peak cycle rate fears. Equities and Multi-Asset: $0.9 billion (5%), with modest active outflows offset by passive indexing.

Regionally, Americas dominated at $11.2 billion (61%), with U.S. wirehouse and RIA channels delivering $7.4 billion, supported by our Aladdin-powered portfolio analytics suite that helped advisors navigate the 4% S&P 500 drawdown in August. EMEA saw $4.6 billion (25%), up 50% YoY, led by UCITS ETF wrappers attracting €2.5 billion from UK DC schemes and German insurers—our sustainable fixed income ETFs here outperformed Vanguard's by 300 bps in flows per Morningstar. APAC contributed $2.6 billion (14%), with Hong Kong and Singapore hubs driving $1.8 billion into China equity recovery plays and yen-hedged global bonds, as regional AUM grew 22% to $45 billion.

These flows translated to ending AUM of $1.47 trillion, up 12% quarter-over-quarter, with market appreciation adding $85 billion and flows providing the organic tailwind. Ex-fee revenue grew 9% to $2.1 billion, with our mix shift toward higher-margin alts and ETFs now at 45% of AUM boosting recurring fee income.

Strategically, we're leaning into digital transformation initiatives, including the rollout of Pinnacle Pulse—a GenAI-enhanced advisor portal—have accelerated retail onboarding by 35%, mirroring Fidelity's Wealthscape gains. ESG integration across 70% of products drove $3.2 billion in sustainable flows, positioning us ahead of peers like State Street in Article 8/9 SFDR compliance. We're addressing active equity outflows (down $1.1 billion YTD) by pivoting to smart beta and factor tilts, with our Quality Momentum strategy launching next quarter.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 net inflows of $16-20 billion, supported by seasonal 401(k) contributions, potential rate cuts unlocking fixed income reallocations, and our $50 billion pipeline of institutional RFPs—strongest in infrastructure and secondaries. Risks remain around U.S. election volatility and China stimulus efficacy, but our diversified platform and 18% organic growth target leave us well-positioned to outpace the industry's flat flows, as projected by McKinsey.

As we wrap up our review of the quarter's financial performance, I'd like to dive deeper into our efficiency ratios, which remain a cornerstone of our competitive edge in the asset management industry. Efficiency ratios, particularly the expense ratio—or more precisely, our total expense ratio (TER)—measure the cost of managing our AUM as a percentage of average AUM. This metric is critical for investors, as it directly impacts net returns, especially in an era of persistent fee compression driven by the rise of passive strategies and regulatory pressures like MiFID II in Europe and the SEC's fee disclosure rules in the U.S.

For Q3 2023, our blended TER across all products stood at 42 basis points (bps), or 0.42%, marking a 12% year-over-year (YoY) improvement from 48 bps in Q3 2022 and a sequential 2 bps decline from Q2's 44 bps. This reflects the powerful scale effects from our record $1.45 trillion in AUM, up 18% YoY, primarily fueled by net inflows of $28 billion into our low-cost ETF suites and strong institutional mandates in fixed income and ESG strategies. For context, our weighted average TER has now trended down from 55 bps five years ago, putting us squarely in line with industry leaders like BlackRock's iShares platform (around 39 bps blended) and ahead of the peer average of 47 bps, per Morningstar's latest data.

By product line: ETFs and Index Funds represented 62% of our AUM at quarter-end, with a TER of just 14 bps—flat YoY but down from 16 bps in 2021. Our flagship Apex Core Equity ETF (APEXQ), tracking a customized MSCI World ex-U.S. index, clocks in at 8 bps, undercutting Vanguard's VTI by 2 bps while delivering beta slippage under 5 bps through our proprietary smart-beta overlays. Inflows here were robust at $19 billion, driven by retail adoption via platforms like Schwab and Fidelity.

Active Mutual Funds and SMAs: At 28% of AUM, the TER here is 68 bps, improved 8% YoY from 74 bps, thanks to fee rebates on high-water-mark performance in our quant-driven equity strategies. However, outflows of $4 billion reflect ongoing active-passive rotation, with clients consolidating into our lower-cost APEX Active Core fund, now at 55 bps post-restructuring.

Alternatives and Institutional: Comprising 10% of AUM ($145 billion), this high-margin segment holds a TER of 92 bps, stable YoY but with gross margins north of 65% due to performance fees averaging 18 bps on our private credit and infrastructure mandates. Institutional wins, like the $5 billion mandate from a CalPERS-like pension fund, underscore our edge here.

Regionally: North America (72% of AUM): TER at 38 bps, benefiting from hyper-competitive ETF flows amid Fed rate hikes and the shift to cash-like products. Our U.S. expense ratio compression outpaced Vanguard's by 3 bps YoY, largely from operational leverage in our robo-advisory platform serving 2.5 million retail clients.

Europe (18% of AUM): TER at 52 bps, pressured by PRIIPs/UCITS packaging costs but improving 10% YoY via our Dublin-domiciled ETF hub. Post-Brexit, we've captured share from Lyxor (now Amundi) with our Euro Stoxx 50 UCITS ETF at 12 bps.

Asia-Pacific (8% of AUM, fastest-growing): TER at 61 bps, reflecting higher distribution costs but 22% YoY AUM growth in Japan and Australia. Initiatives like our Tokyo-listed APEX Nikkei 225 ETF at 15 bps are gaining traction against Nomura's offerings, with regulatory tailwinds from Japan's NISA expansion.

Driving this TER trajectory: Scale economies—AUM growth outpacing expense growth by 3:1 this year, with fixed costs like compliance and middle-office tech amortized over a larger base. Our operating expense ratio—total opex as a percentage of revenue—improved to 62% from 68% YoY, beating our 65% target.

Technical initiatives: We've invested $250 million over the past 18 months in a cloud-native Aladdin-like platform, migrating 85% of our portfolio management and reconciliation workflows to AWS and Snowflake. This has slashed trade execution costs by 25%—from 1.2 bps to 0.9 bps per trade—and enabled real-time TER monitoring via machine learning models that predict fee leakage with 98% accuracy. Additionally, our generative AI pilot for research automation has reduced sell-side analyst costs by 15% in our active equity pods, directly flowing to the TER.

Strategically, product innovation and fee tiering: We've launched six new active ETFs with TERs under 40 bps, blending quant alpha with passive cores—a hybrid model that's resonating amid the active-passive convergence. Looking at peers, while State Street's SPDRs excel in pure beta (10 bps avg), our 15 bps blended active ETF TER offers a compelling alpha capture ratio of 1.12x vs. benchmarks.

Forward-looking, we guide for full-year 2023 blended TER of 41-43 bps, with further compression to sub-40 bps by 2025 as ETF AUM hits 70% of total and our digital transformation yields another 5-7% opex savings. Risks include prolonged fee wars in Europe from UCITS consolidation and potential U.S. DOL fiduciary rule expansions, but our diversified mix and tech moat position us well.

Good afternoon, everyone. As we dive into our financials, I'd like to address a key metric that analysts often focus on in our industry: the compensation ratio, defined as total compensation expense as a percentage of net revenue. This ratio is a critical barometer of our operating leverage in a talent-intensive business like asset management, where human capital drives alpha generation, client retention, and product innovation.

For Q3 2023, our compensation ratio came in at 47.8%, marking a 320 basis point improvement from 51.0% in Q3 2022 and a sequential 110 basis point decline from 48.9% in Q2 2023. On a trailing 12-month basis, it's now 48.5%, down from 53.2% a year ago. This represents our lowest ratio since Q4 2021, pre-dating the volatility of the 2022 bear market. To put this in context, the median comp ratio across the top 20 asset managers—think BlackRock, T. Rowe Price, and Fidelity—hovered around 50-52% in their most recent quarters, per Morningstar data, so we're operating at the more efficient end of the peer spectrum.

Drivers behind this favorable trend: Revenue outperformance. Our net revenue grew 18% year-over-year to $1.42 billion in Q3, fueled by 12% organic AUM growth to $728 billion, average fee compression of just 2 basis points to 48 bps, and a meaningful uptick in performance fees to $285 million—or 20% of total revenue—thanks to strong returns in our long-short equity strategies and private credit sleeves amid the equity rally and narrowing credit spreads. Compensation expense rose only 8% to $679 million, reflecting disciplined expense management.

Comp components: Base salaries increased 4% year-over-year to $320 million, in line with inflation and merit adjustments, but flat sequentially as we lapped last year's hiring surge. Incentive compensation, which is 65% of total comp, was up 12% to $440 million. This includes cash bonuses tied to full-year performance (e.g., our Global Equity Composite beating the MSCI World Index by 420 bps) and equity awards vesting over three years. Notably, performance fees flowed through at a 35% payout rate, below our long-term 40-45% target, prioritizing reinvestment. Benefits and other, at $119 million, benefited from lower healthcare costs and optimized 401(k) matching.

Regionally: In the US, which accounts for 55% of our portfolio manager headcount and 62% of revenue, the ratio was 52%—higher due to intense talent competition in New York and San Francisco. We're paying a 15-20% premium for PMs with quant expertise to staff our AI-driven systematic strategies, similar to what Renaissance or Two Sigma commands. In Europe, at 28% of revenue, the ratio tightened to 44%, aided by MiFID II-driven fee transparency reducing unprofitable mandates and slower hiring amid UCITS ETF outflows. APAC, our growth engine at 15% of AUM with 22% revenue growth, clocked in at 42%, leveraging cost-effective talent in Singapore and Tokyo for our samurai bond and yen carry trade products, though we're investing in Mandarin-fluent relationship managers to capture China's outbound wealth flows.

Strategically, this ratio improvement stems from technology leverage: We've deployed $150 million in tech capex over the past 18 months for our Vertex AI Platform, which automates 30% of middle-office tasks like trade surveillance and ESG scoring. This has deferred 75 hires in operations, directly contributing 80 bps to the ratio compression—echoing BlackRock's Aladdin efficiencies. Talent optimization: Post-2022, we right-sized via natural attrition, reducing headcount by 6% to 4,200 FTEs while upskilling via internal rotations into high-margin private markets (now 18% of AUM). Our comp philosophy ties 40% of variable pay to three-year FCF per share and client net flows, with clawback provisions activated twice this year for underperformance in our EM debt sleeve. Product mix shift: Scaling low-touch ETFs (AUM up 25% to $210 billion, fees at 18 bps) and model portfolios dilutes the comp intensity of high-touch active strategies, where PM comp can exceed 1.5% of fee revenue.

Looking forward, we expect the full-year 2023 comp ratio to land in the 47-49% band, assuming AUM growth of 10-12% and performance fees at 15-20% of revenue. Risks include potential talent wars if the AI equity bubble persists, pushing US salaries higher, or regulatory changes like the SEC's private fund adviser rules inflating compliance headcount. Upside could come from further tech ROI and our $50 billion private assets target by 2025, which boasts 20-30 bps higher fee rates.

We're proud of this discipline—it underscores our ability to deliver 22% adjusted operating margin, up from 17% last year, while investing in the talent that generated 150 bps of net alpha across strategies.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, John. On the investment front, we continue to focus on delivering strong risk-adjusted returns for our clients. Our key strategies performed well, particularly in equities and fixed income. We are navigating the current market environment by leveraging our quant-enhanced models and active duration management. We launched the Apex Global Equity ETF this quarter, and the early reception has been positive, with $8.2 billion in inflows and outperformance versus the S&P 500.
